title: [suite à La "Longue Marche" à travers la théorie de Galois..., pages 650 bis à 787, dont table des matières] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: this page continues the 'Longue Marche' discussion of 'groupes à lacets' of type (g,ν). Such a group is a discrete group isomorphic to the fundamental group of an oriented surface of genus g with ν punctures. It carries a 'loop structure': the distinguished conjugacy classes of loop (parabolic) subgroups or generators around the punctures, compatible with orientation. The previous page defines L_0(π) as the set of admissible loop structures on π, excluding a few small types. It records that a loop structure is recovered from its restrictions to finite-index subgroups: the loop subgroups of π are the intersections with π of the loop subgroups of a finite-index subgroup π_0. It also notes that finite-index normal subgroups are cofinal when π is finitely generated.

This page:
(2) For a finite-index normal subgroup π_i ◁ π, let G_i = π/π_i. It acts by outer automorphisms on π_i, hence on L_0(π_i); L_0^G(π_i) is the fixed set. For π_j ⊂ π_i, restricting a loop structure gives a map L_0^G(π_i) → L_0^G(π_j). Grothendieck defines L(π) = colim over finite-index normal π_i of L_0^G(π_i).
(3) The canonical maps L_0^G(π_i) → L(π) are injective, because restriction of loop structures to finite-index subgroups is injective.
- An element λ ∈ L(π) is an 'L-structure', and (π,λ) is an 'L-group'.
- If λ comes from λ_i ∈ L_0^G(π_i), then π_i is a 'subgroup of definition'. It is regarded as a groupe à lacets through the unique λ_i giving rise to λ.
(4) For π' ⊂ π of finite index there is a canonical induction (restriction) map L(π) → L(π'). It is injective, and its image is the set of L-structures on π' that are invariant under π, 'in an obvious sense' (next page).

Marginal note: if π_i is not normal, define L_0^G(π_i) as the set of λ such that, for every g ∈ π, λ and its conjugate ^gλ induce the same structure on π_i ∩ int(g)(π_i), which is of finite index.

Next page draws the consequences:
- For an extension 1 → π_0 → π → G → 1 with G finite, L-structures on π are the L-structures on π_0 invariant under the outer action G → Autext(π_0).
- π ↦ L(π) is a functor on outer groups with outer isomorphisms as arrows.
- Standard example: π = π_1(X,G;a) for a finite group G acting on a 0-connected 'multiplicité' X.

In modern language, an L-structure is a 'virtual' peripheral/orientation structure. It is defined up to commensurability, making π the orbifold (stack) fundamental group of a 2-dimensional orientable orbifold curve with punctures. Non-effective cases, with a finite normal subgroup acting trivially on π_0, are also allowed. The purpose is to give a purely group-theoretic notion of the discrete fundamental groups of the modular 'multiplicités' M_{g,ν} and their quotients and covers. This is the discrete counterpart of the profinite and Galois-theoretic Teichmüller tower programme.
errors: No real error. Injectivity of (3) and (4) rests on restriction of admissible loop structures to finite-index subgroups being injective. That was asserted on the previous page and is true for the admissible types. For type (1,0) without punctures it would mean recovering an orientation, which is also fine, but that type is excluded anyway.

The colimit over normal finite-index subgroups needs those subgroups to be cofinal among all finite-index subgroups. This always holds (take the normal core). The previous page's appeal to finite generation is only needed to make the definition reasonable, not for cofinality.
'homomorphisme canonique' in (4) is a map of sets, not a homomorphism. This is only a slip of wording.

The definition makes no requirement that π/π_i → Autext(π_i) be injective. So L-groups may contain finite normal subgroups, as in π_0 × Z/2 or SL2(Z) as opposed to PSL2(Z). Such groups correspond to non-effective orbifolds (gerbes) rather than classical Fuchsian groups. This is consistent with stacks having generic stabilizers, such as M_{1,1}, but is not flagged on the page.

Identifying abstract L-groups with fundamental groups of actual orbifold curves, as needed for the 'exemple standard' on the next page, implicitly requires Nielsen realization (Kerckhoff 1983) / Zieschang–Eckmann–Müller. The page does not address this; it only sets up the algebraic definition.

ideas.what: L-structure on a discrete group: a colimit over finite-index normal subgroups of quotient-invariant loop structures, i.e. a commensurability-invariant peripheral/orientation structure
ideas.modern_name: orbifold fundamental group of a 2-dim orientable orbifold with cusps (Fuchsian group with peripheral structure); virtual surface group with peripheral structure
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical Fuchsian/orbifold theory (Poincaré, Fenchel–Nielsen, Thurston's orbifolds 1978); virtual surface groups: Zieschang, Eckmann–Müller
ideas.where_published: Groupes à lacets appear in La Longue Marche (1981) and are alluded to in the Esquisse; the specific colimit definition of L(π) — unsure

ideas.what: Subgroup of definition of an L-group; injectivity of the canonical maps from L_0^G(π_i) to L(π)
ideas.modern_name: a torsion-free finite-index surface subgroup carrying the induced peripheral structure

ideas.what: Induction map L(π) → L(π') for finite-index π', injective with image the π-invariant structures; for G-extensions, L-structures on π are the Autext-invariant L-structures on π_0
ideas.modern_name: descent of peripheral structure along finite covers / Galois descent for orbifold structures

ideas.what: Marginal definition of invariance for non-normal finite-index subgroups via coincidence on π_i ∩ gπ_i g^{-1}

missed.claim: The definition is deliberately commensurability-invariant and functorial for outer isomorphisms. It automatically includes non-effective orbifold groups (finite kernels of π/π_i → Autext(π_i)), such as SL2(Z) as π_1 of the stack M_{1,1}. This is a clean purely group-theoretic axiomatization of the discrete fundamental groups of the 'multiplicités modulaires', parallel to later anabelian/Teichmüller-tower formalisms. Mathematically it is routine and largely implicit in the later literature on orbifold and stack fundamental groups.
missed.quote: on dit que (π,λ) est dit un L-groupe, λ est une L-structure sur π
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Of historical interest only: it shows Grothendieck setting up the discrete (not just profinite) category of 'L-groups' as the natural home for π_1 of modular stacks with generic stabilizers. No new theorem is involved.

deep.surprise_reason: A careful but routine definitional set-up (orbifold/virtual loop structures via a colimit over finite-index subgroups). Its content is standard in Fuchsian and orbifold theory. The only mildly notable feature is the tacit inclusion of non-effective (gerby) cases, consistent with his multiplicités.
transcription_corrections: 'on dit que (π,λ) est dit un L-groupe, [?] λ est une L-structure' should read approximately: 'on dit que λ est une L-structure sur π, (π,λ) est dit un L-groupe'.
'on le considère comme un groupe initiale [?] par l'unique λ_i' is likely 'on le considère comme un groupe à lacets par l'unique λ_i ∈ L_0^G(π_i) donnant naissance à λ'.
The margin '(qui est d'indice fini dans π ...)' is probably '(qui est d'indice fini dans π_i)'; the reading '(ou T [?])' is doubtful.
Margin: 'L_0^G(π_i) comme sous-ensemble de L(π_i)' should probably be L_0(π_i).
